lead: Number theory is the engine room of public-key cryptography. This unit teaches congruences, gcd and inverses, finite fields, primes and primality tests, Fermat and Euler, the Chinese remainder theorem, and quadratic residues. After it you can compute modular inverses and powers, test a number for primality, solve simultaneous congruences, and read the arithmetic inside RSA and ElGamal.
about: This unit gives the number theory that public-key cryptography runs on. Chapter 2.1 sets up congruences and Z_n; 2.2 adds gcd and modular inverses; 2.3 names the groups, rings and fields these operations form. Chapter 2.4 explains primes and fast primality tests, and 2.5 gives Fermat's and Euler's theorems for reducing exponents. Chapter 2.6 combines congruences with the Chinese remainder theorem, and 2.7 covers quadratic residues and the Legendre and Jacobi symbols. The chapters build in that order: each one uses the arithmetic of the earlier ones. Unit 4 then uses this toolkit in RSA, Diffie-Hellman, ElGamal and digital signatures, so treat these as the mathematical base, not the cryptosystems themselves.

chapters.idea: Clock arithmetic: two integers are the same when they leave the same remainder modulo n.
chapters.depth: Definition a ≡ b (mod n); residue classes; Z_n; addition, subtraction and multiplication modulo n; when a has an inverse modulo n (gcd(a,n)=1); fast exponentiation by repeated squaring. Some syllabi call this clock arithmetic or congruences. Keep proofs short and work small moduli by hand.

figure.title: Square-and-multiply for 7²³ mod 13
figure.aria: A table of powers 7, 10, 9, 3, 9 for exponents 1, 2, 4, 8, 16 modulo 13, with the bits of 23 marked for multiplication.

chapters.example: Compute 7²³ mod 13 by square-and-multiply. Write 23 = 16 + 4 + 2 + 1. The powers are 7¹ ≡ 7, 7² ≡ 49 ≡ 10, 7⁴ ≡ 10² = 100 ≡ 9, 7⁸ ≡ 9² = 81 ≡ 3, 7¹⁶ ≡ 3² = 9 ≡ 9 (mod 13). Multiply the powers with bit 1: 7¹⁶ × 7⁴ × 7² × 7¹ ≡ 9 × 9 × 10 × 7. Step by step: 9 × 9 = 81 ≡ 3; 3 × 10 = 30 ≡ 4; 4 × 7 = 28 ≡ 2. So 7²³ ≡ 2 (mod 13).
chapters.trap: Treating a ≡ b as ordinary equality; or reducing an exponent modulo n when the correct reduction is modulo φ(n) (Chapter 2.5).
chapters.prereq: School arithmetic; Unit 1's security goals give context only.
chapters.leave: Modular inverse algorithms to 2.2; primality tests to 2.4; RSA to Unit 4.

chapters.idea: Repeated division finds the gcd, and the extended version also gives the integer coefficients that produce it.
chapters.depth: Euclid's algorithm by repeated division; proof that gcd(a,b) is the last nonzero remainder; extended algorithm returns x, y with ax + by = gcd(a,b); modular inverse when gcd(a,b) = 1; table method; running time O(log min(a,b)). Some syllabi call it extended GCD.
chapters.example: Use the extended Euclidean algorithm on a = 252 and b = 105. Find gcd and integers x, y with 252x + 105y = gcd. Divide: 252 = 2×105 + 42; 105 = 2×42 + 21; 42 = 2×21 + 0. So gcd = 21. Back-substitute: 21 = 105 − 2×42. Replace 42 = 252 − 2×105: 21 = 105 − 2(252 − 2×105) = 5×105 − 2×252. Thus x = −2, y = 5, and 21 = −2×252 + 5×105.
chapters.trap: Losing signs when back-substituting; when gcd is not 1 there is no modular inverse, so do not divide.
chapters.leave: Field arithmetic to 2.3; RSA key setup to Unit 4.

chapters.idea: Groups, rings and fields package the arithmetic rules that cryptosystems assume.
chapters.depth: Group axioms, abelian group, order, cyclic group and generator; ring and field; Z_p is a field exactly when p is prime; finite fields GF(p) and GF(2^m); polynomial arithmetic modulo an irreducible polynomial; AES uses GF(2⁸). If your syllabus lists Cauchy's theorem, state it for a prime dividing the group order. Do not attempt a full classification of finite fields.

figure.aria: Three nested sets: abelian groups contain rings, and rings contain fields; Z_7 sits in the field layer.

chapters.example: Show that Z_7 is a field and find 3⁻¹ mod 7. The elements are 0,1,2,3,4,5,6; addition and multiplication are modulo 7. Since 7 is prime, every nonzero element has an inverse: 1×1=1, 2×4=8≡1, 3×5=15≡1, 4×2=8≡1, 5×3=15≡1, 6×6=36≡1. So 3⁻¹ ≡ 5 (mod 7), and Z_7 is a field.
chapters.trap: Assuming Z_n is a field for every n; it is a field only when n is prime. GF(2^m) is not the same as Z_{2^m}.
chapters.leave: Primality tests to 2.4; AES details to Unit 3.

chapters.idea: Primes are the atoms of the integers; crypto needs large random primes and fast tests that avoid full factoring.
chapters.depth: Prime definition; fundamental theorem of arithmetic; Euclid's proof of infinitude; trial division; Fermat probable-prime test; Carmichael numbers; Miller-Rabin test with n−1 = 2^s d and bases a; error probability per round; generating random primes. Some syllabi call this primality testing algorithm.
chapters.example: Test n = 341 with Miller-Rabin base a = 2. Write n−1 = 340 = 2² × 85, so s = 2 and d = 85. Compute x = 2⁸⁵ mod 341. Since 2¹⁰ = 1024 ≡ 1 (mod 341), 2⁸⁵ = (2¹⁰)⁸ × 2⁵ ≡ 32 (mod 341). This is not 1 or 340, so square once: 32² = 1024 ≡ 1 (mod 341). Now x = 1 and the previous value was 32, not 340, so 341 is composite. Indeed 341 = 11 × 31.
chapters.trap: One Fermat pass is not a proof: 341 passes base 2 but is composite, and Carmichael numbers pass all coprime bases. Miller-Rabin needs several rounds.
chapters.prereq: Chapter 2.1 and 2.2: modular exponentiation and gcd.
chapters.leave: Fermat and Euler theorems to 2.5; RSA prime generation to Unit 4.

chapters.idea: Exponents live in cycles modulo n, so they can be reduced using p−1 or φ(n).
chapters.depth: Fermat's little theorem a^{p−1} ≡ 1 (mod p) when p does not divide a; Euler's totient φ(n); Euler's theorem a^{φ(n)} ≡ 1 (mod n) when gcd(a,n)=1; compute φ(n) from the prime factorization; use these to reduce exponents and find inverses; note that the converse fails. Some syllabi call this the Euler-Fermat theorem.

figure.title: Powers of 3 modulo 7
figure.aria: A row of powers 3, 2, 6, 4, 5, 1 for exponents 1 to 6 modulo 7; the last cell returns to 1 after six steps.

chapters.example: Find 3¹⁰⁰ mod 7. Fermat's little theorem gives 3⁶ ≡ 1 (mod 7) because 7 is prime and 7 does not divide 3. Divide the exponent: 100 = 6×16 + 4. So 3¹⁰⁰ = (3⁶)¹⁶ × 3⁴ ≡ 1¹⁶ × 3⁴ ≡ 81 ≡ 4 (mod 7). Check: 81 = 7×11 + 4.
chapters.trap: Using Fermat's theorem with a composite modulus; or reducing the exponent modulo n instead of modulo p−1 or φ(n).
chapters.prereq: Chapter 2.3 for group order; Chapter 2.4 for primes.
chapters.leave: RSA and ElGamal to Unit 4; CRT to 2.6.

chapters.idea: A congruence modulo a product can be split into congruences modulo coprime factors, then recombined.
chapters.depth: CRT for pairwise coprime moduli; uniqueness modulo the product; construction with M_i and modular inverses; solve two or three congruences; application to RSA decryption speed and secret sharing. State the generalized form but skip the full proof.
chapters.example: Solve x ≡ 2 (mod 3), x ≡ 3 (mod 5), x ≡ 2 (mod 7). The moduli are pairwise coprime, M = 3×5×7 = 105. M₁ = 105/3 = 35; 35 ≡ 2 (mod 3), and 2⁻¹ ≡ 2 (mod 3), so the first term is 2×35×2 = 140. M₂ = 105/5 = 21 ≡ 1 (mod 5), so the second term is 3×21×1 = 63. M₃ = 105/7 = 15 ≡ 1 (mod 7), so the third term is 2×15×1 = 30. Sum = 140 + 63 + 30 = 233 ≡ 23 (mod 105). Check: 23 mod 3 = 2, 23 mod 5 = 3, 23 mod 7 = 2.
chapters.trap: Using non-coprime moduli; the solution is unique only modulo the product, so reduce the final answer modulo M.
chapters.leave: RSA decryption use to Unit 4; polynomial CRT is not needed here.

chapters.idea: Quadratic residues tell which numbers are squares modulo p, and the Legendre and Jacobi symbols test this without listing squares.
chapters.depth: Quadratic residues modulo p; Euler's criterion a^{(p−1)/2} ≡ (a/p) (mod p); Legendre symbol and its properties; quadratic reciprocity statement; Jacobi symbol for odd composite n and its calculation; why Jacobi 1 does not imply a residue. Only a few universities teach this; keep to small examples.

figure.title: Squares modulo 11
figure.aria: A table of x from 1 to 10 and x² modulo 11, showing the residues 1, 4, 9, 5 and 3 repeated in reverse order.

chapters.example: Compute the Legendre symbol (2/11) and decide whether 2 is a quadratic residue modulo 11. Euler's criterion gives (2/11) ≡ 2^{(11−1)/2} = 2⁵ = 32 ≡ 10 ≡ −1 (mod 11). So (2/11) = −1 and 2 is not a quadratic residue modulo 11. The squares modulo 11 are 1, 4, 9, 5, 3, 3, 5, 9, 4, 1, and 2 does not appear.
chapters.trap: A Jacobi symbol of 1 does not prove a quadratic residue when the modulus is composite; the Legendre symbol needs a prime denominator.
chapters.prereq: Chapter 2.5: Euler's criterion uses Fermat's theorem.
chapters.leave: Solovay-Strassen and Tonelli-Shanks to advanced reading or Unit 4; primality testing to 2.4.
